lessons.title: P/E in Depth: Trailing, Forward and the PEG Ratio

children.text: Open any stock on Zerodha Kite or screener.in and the P/E ratio is right there, next to the price. It is the most quoted valuation number in Indian markets, in brokerage reports, business television and every investing WhatsApp group. It is also the most misused. Two stocks with the same P/E can be wildly different bargains, and the same stock can have three different P/Es on the same day depending on whose earnings you use. This lesson makes you precise about all of it.

body.text: A P/E is only as meaningful as the "E" beneath it. Before you compare any two P/E ratios, check which earnings they use, which period they cover, and whether those earnings are normal.

children.text: Two Ways to Calculate the Same Ratio

body.latex: \text{P/E} = \frac{\text{Share price}}{\text{EPS}} = \frac{\text{Market capitalisation}}{\text{Net profit attributable to shareholders}}
body.caption: Both give the same answer when the share count is consistent

children.text: Three details decide which "E" you are really using:
Consolidated or standalone.

Indian companies report both. Standalone excludes subsidiaries, which can be most of the business for groups with large subsidiaries. Use consolidated profit for valuation. screener.in lets you switch between the two, so check which one you are looking at.
Attributable to owners.
Consolidated profit includes the share of subsidiaries owned by minority shareholders. Use profit attributable to the owners of the parent.
Basic or diluted EPS.
Diluted EPS includes shares from stock options and convertibles. For companies with large ESOP pools, it is the more honest figure.
Trailing vs Forward P/E
A
trailing P/E
uses earnings the company has already reported. A
forward P/E
uses earnings analysts expect. In India, forward estimates follow the April to March financial year, so you will see references such as "FY27E EPS" or "20 times FY28E".

markDefs.definition: Share price divided by earnings per share over the last twelve months, usually the sum of the last four reported quarters. Also called TTM (trailing twelve months) P/E.
Share price divided by estimated earnings per share for a future period, usually the next financial year, such as FY27E or FY28E, based on analyst forecasts.

body.caption: One stock at ₹900, three P/E ratios (illustrative, analysts expect 20% EPS growth a year)

columns.label: Trailing P/E
points: Based on: reported, audited or reviewed earnings
Strength: a fact, not a forecast
Weakness: backward-looking, distorted by one-off years
Best for: stable companies and comparing with long historical averages

columns.label: Forward P/E
points: Strength: reflects expected change in the business
Weakness: estimates are often optimistic and revised down
Best for: companies whose earnings are changing fast, with estimates you have checked

body.text: Brokerage reports often quote P/E two years forward because it makes stocks look cheaper: in the table above, the same ₹900 stock drops from 30× to under 21×. Never compare a forward P/E with a historical average that was calculated on trailing earnings. And always ask what earnings growth the forward estimate assumes, and whether the company has ever delivered it.

children.text: Cleaning the "E"
Reported profit often contains items that will not repeat. A P/E calculated on it can make an expensive stock look cheap, or a cheap one expensive. The main items to strip out:

body.caption: Adjustments to reported profit before calculating P/E

cells: Profit on sale of land, a subsidiary or a stake in another company
Impairment of goodwill or assets, one-time restructuring costs
Add back, net of tax, if genuinely non-recurring
Deferred tax remeasurement, such as when many companies moved to the lower corporate tax rate introduced in September 2019
Remove, and use a normal tax rate
Interest on surplus cash and mutual fund gains booked in other income
Keep, but consider a cash-adjusted P/E
Record steel or sugar profits in a boom year

children.text: Worked example: Sahyadri Auto Components

Sahyadri Auto Components Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed maker of engine parts. Its shares trade at ₹450, with 12 crore shares outstanding, a market capitalisation of ₹5,400 crore. Last year's reported consolidated PAT was ₹240 crore. The notes show an exceptional gain of ₹80 crore on sale of surplus land near Pune, taxed at ₹20 crore. The company also holds ₹600 crore of surplus cash in liquid mutual funds and deposits.

body.caption: Sahyadri Auto Components: from reported P/E to clean P/E (₹ crore)

children.text: The stock screens at 22.5× on reported numbers. The operating business, the part that actually makes engine parts, is priced at 32.3× its recurring profit. The cash-adjusted figure assumes the cash earns 7.0% before tax, or 5.25% after 25% tax. Cash earning 5.25% after tax is effectively valued at 19.0 times its income. So removing cash raises the P/E of any stock trading above about 19.0×, as Sahyadri does, and lowers it for stocks trading below that. For highly rated, cash-rich companies, such as many Indian IT services firms, the operating business is usually more expensive than the headline P/E suggests.

body.text: A stock screener sorting by P/E will put companies with one-off gains at the top of the "cheap" list. Before acting on any low P/E, open the latest annual report and quarterly results and look for the words "exceptional items" and "other income".

children.text: What P/E Should a Company Deserve?
Chapter 1 showed that a P/E is a compressed DCF. For a company whose earnings grow at a steady rate g forever, with return on equity ROE and cost of equity Ke, the justified forward P/E is:

body.caption: The numerator is the payout ratio needed to sustain growth g at return ROE
Justified forward P/E at a 12% cost of equity: ROE (rows) × sustainable growth (columns)

children.text: Two lessons stand out. First, higher ROE always supports a higher P/E at the same growth, because less profit has to be reinvested. Second, growth only raises the justified P/E strongly when ROE is well above the cost of equity: at a 15% ROE, moving from 4% to 8% growth takes the P/E from 9.2× to 11.7×, while at 30% ROE it goes from 10.8× to 18.3×. Note that 8% growth forever is aggressive, so treat the last column as an upper bound.
The PEG Ratio
Because P/E rises with growth, investors often divide one by the other. The
PEG ratio
, popularised by the fund manager Peter Lynch, adjusts P/E for expected growth.

markDefs.definition: P/E ratio divided by the expected annual EPS growth rate expressed as a whole number. A P/E of 30 with 20% expected growth gives a PEG of 1.5.

body.caption: Growth is usually a three- to five-year forward EPS CAGR

children.text: The popular rule of thumb says a PEG of 1 is fair value, below 1 is cheap and above 1 is expensive. It is a useful first filter and a poor final answer.

body.caption: Three fictional companies with similar or equal PEG ratios

children.text: Companies A and C both have a PEG of 2.00. They are nothing alike. A must sustain 30% growth for many years to justify 60 times earnings, while C's modest multiple rests on steady, low-risk cash flows. PEG ignores how long growth lasts, how much capital it needs, and how risky it is.
What PEG is fair? It depends on duration

Use a two-stage model instead of the rule of thumb. Assume a company with a 25% ROE and a 12% cost of equity grows EPS at a high rate for a number of years, then at 6% forever, reinvesting just enough to fund its growth. The fair trailing P/E, and therefore the fair PEG, depends heavily on how long high growth lasts.

body.caption: Fair trailing P/E and PEG from a two-stage model (ROE 25%, Ke 12%, then 6% growth forever)

children.text: The same 20% growth rate justifies a very different P/E, and PEG, depending on whether it lasts five years or ten. And a slower grower can deserve a higher PEG than a faster one, because PEG divides by growth in a straight line while value does not behave that way. A PEG of 1 is not a law of valuation. It is a shortcut that works only by coincidence.
P/E for the Whole Market
The same discipline applies to the Nifty 50 P/E, which is widely tracked as a market valuation signal.

stats.context: Trailing P/E, before the global financial crisis

stats.context: Earnings collapsed in the Covid year, not only prices rising

body.text: Index P/E history needs care. The spike in early 2021 came largely from a temporary collapse in earnings, the "E", during the pandemic year. NSE also changed the Nifty's P/E calculation from standalone to consolidated earnings in 2021, which lowered reported P/Es and makes older and newer figures not directly comparable. Always check the basis before comparing today's index P/E with history.

children.text: When P/E Works and When It Fails

cells: Stable, profitable businesses: FMCG, IT services, pharma, consumer durables
Cyclicals near peak or trough earnings: steel, cement, sugar
P/E on normalised earnings, EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle EBITDA

children.text: Check Your Understanding

body.title: Forward P/E
body.prompt: A pharma company's shares trade at ₹1,200. Analysts expect EPS of ₹48 for FY27. What is its FY27E forward P/E?
body.explanation: Forward P/E = ₹1,200 ÷ ₹48 = 25.0×. Before using it, compare the FY27E EPS with the trailing EPS to see how much growth the estimate assumes.

body.title: Clean the earnings
body.prompt: A chemicals company has 20 crore shares trading at ₹300. Reported PAT is ₹400 crore, including a ₹100 crore exceptional gain on selling a stake in a joint venture, on which it paid ₹25 crore of tax. What is its P/E on adjusted earnings? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Market cap = 20 crore × ₹300 = ₹6,000 crore. Adjusted PAT = ₹400 - (₹100 - ₹25) = ₹325 crore. Adjusted P/E = ₹6,000 ÷ ₹325 = 18.5×, compared with 15.0× on reported profit.

body.title: The PEG trap
body.question: Two stocks both have a PEG ratio of 1.0. Stock X has a P/E of 40 and expected growth of 40% for the next three years. Stock Y has a P/E of 15 and expected growth of 15% for the next ten years, with a higher ROE. What is the best conclusion?
options: They are equally attractive because their PEG ratios are equal
Stock X is cheaper because it grows faster
They are not comparable on PEG alone; Y's longer, better-funded growth is likely worth more per unit of growth than X's short burst
Both are overvalued because PEG should always be below 1
body.explanation: PEG ignores how long growth lasts, how much reinvestment it needs and how risky it is. Three years of 40% growth followed by a slowdown can be worth much less than ten years of 15% growth at a high ROE. Equal PEGs can hide very different values.

body.title: Name the P/E
body.textWithBlank: A P/E calculated using the sum of EPS from the last four reported quarters is called a ___ P/E.
body.explanation: Trailing, or TTM, P/E uses reported earnings over the last twelve months. Forward P/E uses estimates.

body.title: Cheap against its own history?
body.scenario: Ishaan, a Jaipur-based chartered accountant, reads a brokerage note on a listed hotel chain: "The stock trades at 22× FY28E earnings, a steep discount to its 5-year average P/E of 45×. BUY." Checking screener.in, he finds that the 5-year average was calculated on trailing earnings, which included two pandemic years with very low profits. The FY28E EPS estimate is 2.1 times the latest trailing EPS. Last year's reported profit also included a one-time gain from selling a property in Goa.
body.prompt: What is wrong with the brokerage's comparison, and how should Ishaan rebuild it?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Mismatched bases. A two-year forward P/E is being compared with a historical average calculated on trailing earnings. Forward P/Es are almost always lower than trailing P/Es for a growing company, so the "discount" is partly created by the method.
2. A distorted historical average. The 5-year average includes pandemic years when hotel earnings collapsed, which pushed P/Es to extreme levels. The average of 45× is not a normal benchmark.
3. A demanding estimate. FY28E EPS is 2.1 times trailing EPS, which implies roughly 45% annual growth over two years. The 22× multiple is only as reliable as that estimate.
4. Unclean current earnings. Trailing profit includes a one-time property gain, which flatters the latest EPS and the base from which growth is projected.

How to rebuild it:
1. Compare like with like: trailing P/E on clean earnings against a historical trailing average that excludes the pandemic years, or forward P/E against historical forward P/Es.
2. Remove the Goa property gain from trailing earnings.
3. Test the FY28E estimate against the company's room count, occupancy and room rate history.
4. Cross-check with EV/EBITDA, which is commonly used for hotels given their capital intensity and debt.

cards.definition: Price ÷ EPS from the last four reported quarters.
Price ÷ estimated EPS for a future year, such as FY27E.
P/E on profit with one-off gains and losses removed, net of tax.
(Market cap - surplus cash) ÷ (adjusted PAT - post-tax income on that cash). Values the operating business alone.
(1 - g/ROE) ÷ (Ke - g). The P/E a company deserves given its growth, returns and risk.
P/E ÷ expected EPS growth (%). A quick growth adjustment that ignores duration, reinvestment and risk.

points: Use consolidated profit attributable to shareholders and, where relevant, diluted EPS.
Trailing P/E uses reported earnings; forward P/E uses estimates. Never compare one with a historical average of the other.
Clean the earnings: remove exceptional items and tax one-offs, and consider a cash-adjusted P/E for cash-rich companies.
A justified P/E rises with ROE and sustainable growth and falls with the cost of equity.
PEG adjusts for growth but ignores its duration, cost and risk. A PEG of 1 is a rule of thumb, not fair value.
P/E fails for cyclicals at extremes, loss-makers, banks and holding companies. Use the right alternative.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Sahyadri Auto Components Ltd, the other companies described and the individuals named are fictional, and their figures are illustrative. Nifty 50 P/E figures are approximate and depend on the calculation basis. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
